title: NY Post: CIA 'Ghost Murmur' tool pairing quantum magnetometry with AI located downed F-15E officer 'Dude 44 Bravo' in Iran before his 4 April 2026 rescue; anonymous-sourced, disputed by physicists
summary: The rescue is official (Ratcliffe, 6 Apr 2026). The tool rests on two anonymous Post sources; Lockheed declined comment; Trump called it 'very important'; physicists say the physics fails.
account: The OECD AI Incidents Monitor record 2026-04-08-d905 says that the CIA deployed 'Ghost Murmur', using quantum magnetometry and AI algorithms to detect heartbeats, to locate and rescue a downed US pilot in Iran, and lists 40-odd Chinese, Korean, Italian and Spanish syndications. The rescue itself is documented: Air & Space Forces Magazine (6 Apr 2026) reports from the White House briefing that an F-15E was shot down in the early hours of 3 April local time, that the two crew ejected with rescue beacons active (Gen. Caine), that CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the agency used human assets and 'sophisticated intelligence technologies' and confirmed on the morning of 4 April that the weapons systems officer was alive in a mountain crevice, that a camera was trained on his suspected position from 40 miles away until he stood up after about 45 minutes, and that the extraction followed that night. The New York Post (Steven Nelson, 7 Apr 2026, exclusive) reports from 'two sources close to the breakthrough' that the CIA used Ghost Murmur, which 'uses long-range quantum magnetometry to find the electromagnetic signal of a human heartbeat and pairs the data with artificial intelligence software to isolate the signature from background noise', in its first field use; the sources say it was developed by Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works, 'The company declined to comment', the airman's CSEL beacon is described as giving a secondary confirmation layer, and Trump and Ratcliffe only 'alluded' to secret technology. On 8 April the Post reported that Trump told it by phone that the tool 'was very important. The CIA was fantastic', while physicists Thad Walker (Wisconsin) and others said that detection at even 100 metres with NV-diamond magnetometers 'would be astounding'. Scientific American (Deni Ellis Béchard, 8 Apr 2026) quotes Vanderbilt's John Wikswo that the heart's field is 'just barely detectable' at 10 centimetres and concludes that Ghost Murmur 'as publicly described, finds no support in decades of peer-reviewed physics, even with the help of AI'; Military.com (18 Apr 2026) says that the 40-mile heartbeat claim 'remains unverified and inconsistent with publicly documented physics' and that no agency has confirmed the capability; The Quantum Insider (8 Apr 2026) finds no published research near the described performance; Ynet and CTech (9 Apr 2026) and Diario Panorama (10 Apr 2026, relaying The Times and Scientific American) repeat the doubts. The Monitor's listed sources are derivative of the Post. No CIA, DoD, White House transcript or Lockheed confirmation of the tool exists in any fetched source.
purpose: Per the Post's sources, a tool built to find a human heartbeat at distance for intelligence collection and personnel recovery, tested on Black Hawk helicopters; its stated purpose is exactly the use claimed.
system: 'Ghost Murmur': long-range quantum (nitrogen-vacancy diamond) magnetometry paired with AI software that isolates heartbeat signatures from background noise, as described by the NY Post's anonymous sources
developer: Lockheed Martin Skunk Works, per two NY Post sources; the company declined to comment
deployer: US Central Intelligence Agency, per the NY Post; the CIA and White House named no tool
domain: Defence and intelligence: combat search and rescue
taxonomy_note: Classified as the claim is made (an airman located and recovered alive). No defence or rescue type exists among the six; efficiency of the search is the nearest fit. The outcome (rescue, no US casualties) is official, so a personal depth is given; the attribution to Ghost Murmur is not. Unsupported: the tool's existence, mechanism and use rest on two anonymous NY Post sources; Lockheed Martin declined to comment; Ratcliffe and the briefing named no tool; Trump's on-record words to the Post are that it 'was very important' and that 'Nobody even knows what it is'. Contradicted: Wikswo (Scientific American), Walker (NY Post, 8 Apr) and Military.com say that detecting a cardiac magnetic field at kilometres is outside known physics; Walker's best guess is a drone-mounted magnetometer array close to the source. The Post itself notes that the airman's CSEL beacon was active and 'gave operators a secondary confirmation layer', and Air & Space Forces reports a camera trained on his position from 40 miles.

ratings.reason: The weapons systems officer was found alive on 4 April 2026 and extracted with no US casualties, per Ratcliffe and Trump; whether Ghost Murmur produced the find rests on the Post's anonymous sources and Trump's 'very important', with physicists disputing the described mechanism and a beacon and a long-range camera also in play.
No source quantifies the tool's contribution to the search beyond Trump's remark; the mission also used human assets, deception, a camera at 40 miles and the airman's beacon.

ai_role.statement: The only description of an AI role is the Post's sources' statement that artificial intelligence software isolates the heartbeat signature from background noise. No official, technical or manufacturer source confirms the tool, its AI component or its use; Lockheed declined to comment; the CIA named no tool. Scientific American's experts say that the public description fails 'even with the help of AI'. The AI's contribution cannot be assessed.

headline: NY Post says Ghost Murmur found downed F-15E officer; disputed
metric: a camera was trained on his suspected position from 40 miles away
brief: In April 2026 a United States F-15E was shot down over Iran and its weapons systems officer was found alive the next morning; that much is established by the White House briefing and by CIA Director Ratcliffe. The claim that a quantum sensor with AI, 'Ghost Murmur', found him is the part that travelled: two anonymous sources in a New York Post exclusive, a presidential 'very important', and forty-odd syndications in four languages. Scientific American and Military.com then reported that the described detection at 40 miles finds no support in published physics; Lockheed Martin declined to comment and no agency confirmed the tool. The case matters now because claims about AI in military operations are moving faster than the evidence for them, and this database rates them accordingly: The −5 is the officer's life, which is documented, while the AI's part is unassessed. Until an official or technical source names the tool, this is a rescue with a story attached.
